subtitle: A standardized way to monitor and manage OSPF routers using SNMP.

tldr.problem: OSPF routers need to be monitored and configured remotely, but there is no standard set of management objects for network administrators to query.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1248 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) with dozens of objects that represent OSPF router state, configuration, areas, neighbors, interfaces, and link state databases, all accessible via SNMP.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was superseded by RFC 1252 and later RFC 1850, but it established the pattern for OSPF network management.

today: RFC 1248 defined the first MIB for OSPF management but was quickly updated. RFC 1252 extended it and later RFC 1850 became the standard. While RFC 1248 itself is no longer the current specification, the structure and many of the objects it defined remain in use in modern OSPF management implementations.

sections.title: Overview of the OSPF MIB
sections.content:
This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB)—a collection of managed objects—for monitoring and managing OSPF Version 2 routers using SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol. The MIB allows network administrators to query router state, configure OSPF parameters, and track the OSPF routing protocol's operation.

The RFC documents the structure of this MIB, defining the objects and their syntax using Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1). It covers global OSPF parameters, areas, the link state database, interfaces, neighbors, and virtual links. Many objects are read-write, allowing network administrators to modify OSPF configuration remotely, though implementations may choose to make them read-only for security.

RFC 1248 was the initial specification. It was later updated by RFC 1349 and eventually replaced by RFC 1252 and RFC 1850.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a list of things you can ask an OSPF router about its configuration and operation, and some things you can change.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The MIB is organized into eleven sections:

General Variables contain global OSPF parameters like the router ID, whether OSPF is enabled or disabled, the version number, and whether the router is an area border router or autonomous system border router. They also track statistics like the number of external link state advertisements.

The Area Data Structure describes each area the router participates in, including the area ID, authentication type, and statistics like the count of border routers and link state advertisements in that area. A separate Area Stub Metric Table specifies the metrics that area border routers advertise into stub areas.

The Link State Database contains the actual link state advertisements (LSAs) the router has received, indexed by area, type, link state ID, and router ID. This is primarily for debugging and verification of routing correctness.

The Address Range Table lists network address ranges configured for summarization, and the Host Table lists any host routes the router advertises. The Interface Table describes all IP interfaces configured for OSPF, and the separate Interface Metric Table allows per-interface metrics for different types of service.

Finally, Neighbor and Virtual Neighbor Tables track the OSPF neighbors the router has discovered or configured.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is organized into buckets: global settings, areas, neighborhoods, interfaces, databases, and configurations for special cases.

sections.title: Managing OSPF Configuration
sections.content:
Many objects in the MIB are read-write, allowing network administrators to configure OSPF. For example, an administrator can set the router ID, enable or disable OSPF entirely, control whether the router is an autonomous system border router, configure areas and their authentication, and modify interface metrics.

The MIB uses a common pattern called conceptual row creation. When creating a new table entry (such as a new area), the manager sends a Set request with values for the row's columns. The MIB defines default values (DEFVAL) for objects that are not specified, allowing simple configuration with a single Set request.

For example, enabling OSPF on a router can be as simple as setting ospfAdminStat to enabled. The router will automatically discover IP interfaces, create corresponding OSPF interfaces, create areas as needed, and assign default timers and metrics based on interface speed.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send commands to the router to tell it how to route, and the MIB lets you set defaults so you don't have to specify everything.

sections.title: Representing OSPF State
sections.content:
The MIB defines several important data types and fields:

Area ID and Router ID are stored as 32-bit integers (like an IP address), but they represent logical identifiers, not IP addresses. Metrics are 16-bit or 24-bit unsigned integers representing path costs. Timers are measured in seconds.

Each table entry in the MIB is indexed by one or more of these fields. For example, the Interface Metric Table is indexed by interface index and Type-of-Service. The Link State Database is indexed by area ID, LSA type, link state ID, and router ID.

The MIB also defines status fields to indicate whether entries are valid, enabled, or disabled. For example, setting ospfAreaStatus to invalid causes an area to become inoperative.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB describes how to identify and index different pieces of router state, like areas and interfaces, so you can look them up and modify them.

sections.title: Debugging and Statistics
sections.content:
Beyond configuration, the MIB provides visibility into OSPF operation. Global variables count events like the number of times the SPF (shortest path first) algorithm has run in each area, the number of new link state advertisements originated, and the number received.

The Link State Database object provides the full text of every LSA in the router's database, allowing managers to verify that databases are synchronized across the network and to debug routing problems. For example, if a manager suspects a routing loop or incorrect routes, examining the LSAs in each router's database can reveal the root cause.

Administrators can also query interface statistics like the number of OSPF packets sent and received, error counts, and the state of each neighbor relationship (Down, Attempt, Init, Two-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, Full).
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB lets you see what the router is doing: how many times it recalculated routes, what messages it has received, and the status of each connection to a neighbor.

sections.title: Implementation and Standards
sections.content:
This MIB is defined as an experimental portion of the Internet management framework. It uses ASN.1 and is encoded using the Basic Encoding Rules defined by SNMP. The RFC specifies the syntax of each object using textual conventions like TruthValue, Status, and Counter.

The RFC emphasizes robustness through default values and the Robustness Principle (from RFC 791): management stations should be liberal in what they accept, and agents should be conservative in what they send. For example, when creating a row, agents should accept Set requests with as few columns as needed, and should provide sensible defaults for omitted values.

RFC 1248 was later updated by RFC 1349 and eventually superseded by RFC 1252, which extended the MIB, and later by RFC 1850, which added support for OSPF MD5 authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: This follows the standard pattern for describing router settings in a way that all network management tools can understand, and it emphasizes being forgiving if things are missing or wrong.
